look_here_first: Start with the opposite compound leaves: boxelder is a maple that often looks like an ash. Then confirm the paired V-shaped samaras. In season, note that the tree is dioecious and the small flowers lack petals.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves opposite and usually odd-pinnately compound with 3 or 5 leaflets

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaflets variably lobed or unlobed, often coarsely serrate

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: dioecious: staminate and pistillate flowers occur on separate trees

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: pistillate ovary develops two conspicuous wings

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: fruit splits into a paired set of one-seeded winged mericarps/samaras, commonly hanging in a V

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Opposite compound leaves are the first clue. This is unusual-looking for a maple and is why boxelder is often mistaken for an ash.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Flowers are small and lack a corolla. Male and female flowers occur on separate trees.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: The fruit is a schizocarp of two winged one-seeded mericarps, producing the familiar paired maple samara.

key_traits.label: Field tip
key_traits.text: When a tree has opposite compound leaves, check the fruit before calling it an ash. Paired samaras point to Acer negundo; Fraxinus produces single samaras.
